title: Moses spoke of the fallen one long before the Greeks
source_text: Ὅρα οὖν εἰ μὴ ὁ ἐγκαλῶν ἡμῖν (ὡς) σφαλλομένοις ἀσεβέστατα καὶ ἀποπεπλανημένοις θείων αἰνιγμάτων αὐτὸς σαφῶς σφάλλεται, μὴ κατανοήσας ὅτι τὰ πολλῷ οὐ μόνον Ἡρακλείτου καὶ Φερεκύδου ἀρχαιότερα ἀλλὰ καὶ Ὁμήρου Μωϋσέως γράμματα εἰσήγαγε τὸν περὶ τοῦ πονηροῦ τούτου καὶ ἐκπεσόντος τῶν οὐρανίων λόγον. ὁ γὰρ „ὄφις“ παρ᾿ ὃν ὁ παρὰ τῷ Φερεκύδῃ γέγονεν Ὀφιονεὺς, αἴτιος γενόμενος τοῦ ἐκβληθῆναι τοῦ θείου παραδείσου τὸν ἄνθρωπον, τοιαῦτά τινα αἰνίσσεται, ἐπαγγελίᾳ θεότητος καὶ μειζόνων ἀπατήσας τὸ θηλύτερον γένος· ᾧ συνηκολουθηκέναι λέγεται καὶ ὁ ἀνήρ. καὶ ὁ ἐν τῇ Μωϋσέως δὲ Ἐξόδῳ ὀλεθρευτὴς τίς ἄλλος εἴη ἢ ὁ τοῦ ὀλέθρου τοῖς πειθομένοις αὐτῷ καὶ μὴ ἀνθισταμένοις αὐτοῦ τῇ κακίᾳ καὶ μὴ ἀνταγωνιζομένοις αἴτιος; ἔτι δὲ (ὁ) ἐν τῷ Λευϊτικῷ ἀποπομπαῖος, ὃν ἡ Ἑβραϊκὴ γραφὴ ὠνόμασεν Ἀζαζὴλ, οὐδεὶς ἕτερος ἦν· (ὃν) ἀποπέμπεσθαι καὶ ἀποτροπιάζεσθαι ἔδει τὸν κλῆρον ἔχοντα ἐν ἐρήμῳ· πάντες γὰρ οἱ τῆς τοῦ χείρονος διὰ τὴν κακίαν μερίδος ἐναντίοι ὄντες τοῖς ἀπὸ τοῦ κλήρου τοῦ θεοῦ ἔρημοί εἰσι θεοῦ. ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ ἐν τοῖς Κριταῖς υἱοὶ Βελίαρ τίνος ἄλλου ἢ τούτου λέγονται εἶναι υἱοὶ διὰ τὴν πονηρίαν; σαφῶς δὲ παρὰ ταῦτα πάντα ἐν τῷ ἀρχαιοτέρῳ καὶ Μωϋσέως αὐτοῦ Ἰὼβ „ὁ διάβολος“ ἀναγέγραπται παρίστασθαι τῷ θεῷ καὶ αἰτεῖν τὴν κατὰ τοῦ Ἰὼβ ἐξουσίαν, ἵν᾿ αὐτὸν περιβάλῃ περιστάσεσι βαρυτάταις, πρώτῃ μὲν τῇ κατὰ πάντων τῶν ὑπαρχόντων αὐτῷ καὶ τῶν τέκνων αὐτοῦ ἀπωλείᾳ, δευτέρᾳ δὲ κατὰ τὸ περιβαλεῖν αὐτὸν ἀγρίῳ ἐλέφαντι, τῷ οὕτω καλουμένῳ νοσήματι, πᾶν τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Ἰώβ. ἐῶ γὰρ τὰ ἀπὸ τῶν εὐαγγελίων περὶ τοῦ πειράζοντος τὸν σωτῆρα διαβόλου, ἵνα μὴ δόξω ἀπὸ νεωτέρων γραφῶν φέρειν τὰ περὶ τοῦ ζητουμένου πρὸς τὸν Κέλσον. καὶ ἐν τοῖς τελευταίοις δὲ τοῦ Ἰὼβ, ἐν οἷς ὁ κύριος διὰ λαίλαπος καὶ νεφελῶν εἶπε τῷ Ἰὼβ τὰ ἀναγεγραμμένα ἐν τῇ ὁμωνύμῳ βίβλῳ αὐτοῦ, οὐκ ὀλίγα ἐστὶ περὶ δράκοντος εἰρημένα λαβεῖν. οὔπω λέγω καὶ τὰ ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰεζεκιὴλ ὡς περὶ „Φαραὼ“ ἢ „Ναβουχοδονόσορ“ ἢ ἄρχοντος „Τύρου“, ἢ τὰ ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἡσαΐου, ἐν οἷς θρηνεῖται ὁ βασιλεὺς Βαβυλῶνος· ἀφ᾿ ὧν οὐκ ὀλίγα τις ἂν μανθάνοι περὶ τῆς κακίας, ποίαν ἔσχεν ἀρχὴν καὶ γένεσιν, καὶ ὅτι ἀπό τινων πτεροῤῥυησάντων καὶ κατακολουθησάντων τῷ πρώτῳ πτεροῤῥυήσαντι ὑπέστη ἡ κακία.
pass_a_gloss: See (ὁράω) then whether the one accusing (ἐγκαλέω) us as erring (σφάλλομαι) most impiously and having wandered away (ἀποπλανάω) from divine riddles does not himself clearly (σαφῶς) err, not having perceived (κατανοέω) that the writings (γράμματα) of Moses, much older not only than Heraclitus and Pherecydes but also than Homer, introduced (εἰσάγω) the account (λόγος) about this evil one (πονηρός) and fallen (ἐκπίπτω) from the heavenly things (οὐράνια). For the 'serpent' (ὄφις), from which Pherecydes's Ophioneus came to be, having become cause (αἴτιος) of the man (ἄνθρωπος) being cast out (ἐκβάλλω) of the divine paradise (παράδεισος), hints at such things, having deceived (ἀπατάω) the female kind (θηλύτερον γένος) with a promise (ἐπαγγελία) of godhead (θεότης) and greater things; whom the husband (ἀνήρ) also is said to have followed (συνακολουθέω). And the destroyer (ὀλεθρευτής) in Moses's Exodus, who else would he be than the cause of destruction (ὄλεθρος) to those obeying (πείθομαι) him and not resisting (ἀνθίσταμαι) his wickedness (κακία) and not struggling against (ἀνταγωνίζομαι) it? Further, the one sent away (ἀποπομπαῖος) in Leviticus, whom the Hebrew scripture named Azazel, was no other; whom the one having the lot (κλῆρος) had to be sent off (ἀποπέμπω) and averted (ἀποτροπιάζομαι) in the wilderness (ἔρημος); for all those of the portion (μερίς) of the worse (χείρων) through wickedness, being opposite to those from the lot of God, are deserted (ἔρημοι) of God. But also the sons of Belial (Βελίαρ) in Judges, of whom else than this one are they said to be sons through wickedness (πονηρία)? Clearly beyond all these, in Job, older even than Moses himself, 'the devil' is recorded (ἀναγράφω) standing beside (παρίσταμαι) God and asking (αἰτέω) the authority (ἐξουσία) against Job, that he might surround (περιβάλλω) him with heaviest circumstances (περίστασις): first the destruction (ἀπώλεια) of all his possessions (ὑπάρχοντα) and his children (τέκνα), second the surrounding of the whole body of Job with savage elephantiasis (ἄγριος ἐλέφας), the disease (νόσημα) so called. For I let go (ἐάω) the things from the Gospels about the devil tempting (πειράζω) the Saviour (σωτήρ), that I may not seem to bring from newer writings (νεώτεραι γραφαί) things on the question against Celsus. And in the last parts of Job, in which the Lord through whirlwind (λαῖλαψ) and clouds spoke to Job the things recorded in his same-named book, it is possible to take not few things said about the dragon (δράκων). I do not yet say the things from Ezekiel as about 'Pharaoh' or 'Nebuchadnezzar' or ruler (ἄρχων) of 'Tyre', or the things from Isaiah in which the king of Babylon is lamented (θρηνέω); from which one would learn not few things about wickedness, what beginning (ἀρχή) and origin (γένεσις) it had, and that wickedness came to exist (ὑφίσταμαι) from some having shed their wings (πτερορρυέω) and having followed (κατακολουθέω) the first who shed his wings.
pass_b_english: See, then, whether the man who charges us with most impious errors and with having strayed from divine riddles is not himself plainly in error. He has not perceived that the writings of Moses, which are much older not only than Heraclitus and Pherecydes but even than Homer, brought in the account of this evil one who fell from the heavenly places. For the “serpent” (Genesis 3:1), from whom Pherecydes’ Ophioneus derives, and who became the cause of man’s being cast out of the divine paradise (Genesis 3:23–24), hints at something of this kind: he deceived womankind with a promise of divinity and of greater things (Genesis 3:5), and the man is said to have followed her (Genesis 3:6).

And the destroyer in Moses’ Exodus (Exodus 12:23): who else could he be but the one who causes destruction for those who obey him and do not resist his wickedness or struggle against it? Again, the one sent away in Leviticus, whom the Hebrew text named Azazel (Leviticus 16:8–10), was no other than he. The one that bore his lot had to be sent away into the wilderness and driven off to avert evil; for all who belong, through their wickedness, to the portion of the worse one stand opposed to those who are of God’s lot, and are deserts, empty of God. And the sons of Belial in Judges (Judges 19:22): whose sons are they said to be, because of their wickedness, if not his?

But more clearly than all these, in Job, who is older even than Moses himself, “the devil” is recorded as standing before God (Job 1:6; 2:1) and asking for power against Job (Job 1:9–12; 2:4–6), so as to surround him with the heaviest calamities: first the loss of all his possessions and of his children (Job 1:13–19), and second the covering of Job’s whole body with a savage elephantiasis, as the disease is called (Job 2:7). For I pass over what the Gospels say about the devil who tempted the Saviour (Matthew 4:1–11; Luke 4:1–13), so as not to seem to bring proof against Celsus on the point in question from more recent writings. In the last parts of Job too, where the Lord spoke to Job through whirlwind and clouds (Job 38:1) the words recorded in the book that bears his name, one may find not a few things said about the dragon (Job 41:1–34).

I say nothing yet of the passages in Ezekiel that speak as though of “Pharaoh” (Ezekiel 29:2–3; 32:2), or “Nebuchadnezzar,” or the ruler of “Tyre” (Ezekiel 28:2–19), or of those in Isaiah where the king of Babylon is lamented (Isaiah 14:4–21). From them one could learn not a little about wickedness: what beginning and origin it had, and that wickedness came into being from some who shed their wings and followed the first who shed his wings.

choices.choice: Exodus 12:23: the Septuagint has τὸν ὀλεθρεύοντα (‘the destroyer’); Origen uses ὀλεθρευτής. Leviticus 16:8–10: the Septuagint calls the goat ὁ ἀποπομπαῖος (‘the one sent away’); Origen notes the Hebrew name Azazel. τὸν κλῆρον ἔχοντα is rendered ‘the one that bore his lot’ (the goat of Leviticus 16:10, not named in the Greek here). ἔρημοί εἰσι θεοῦ plays on ἐν ἐρήμῳ (‘in the wilderness’); rendered ‘are deserts, empty of God’ to keep the play. Judges 19:22: the Alexandrian text of the Septuagint reads υἱοὶ Βελιαλ, the Vatican text υἱοὶ παρανόμων; Origen’s Βελίαρ is the form of 2 Corinthians 6:15; given the familiar English ‘Belial’; compare also Judges 20:13. Job: the Septuagint has the devil ‘stand before the Lord’ (Job 1:6; 2:1); the ‘savage elephantiasis’ is Origen’s name for the ‘evil sore’ (ἕλκει πονηρῷ) of Job 2:7. The age of Job relative to Moses is Origen’s own claim. The dragon passage is Septuagint Job 40:25–41:26 (δράκοντα, 40:25), which is English Job 41:1–34; Septuagint Job 38:1 reads διὰ λαίλαπος καὶ νεφῶν. Ezekiel: Pharaoh as the great dragon is Ezekiel 29:3 and 32:2; the ruler and king of Tyre is Ezekiel 28:2–19. No single Ezekiel passage about Nebuchadnezzar fits this argument (he is named at Ezekiel 26:7; 29:18–19; 30:10), so no inline citation is given for him. Isaiah 14:4 introduces the lament over the king of Babylon. πτερορρυέω (‘shed the wings’) is Plato’s word for the fall of the soul (Plato, Phaedrus 246c, 248c); it is an echo of vocabulary, not a quotation, so it is noted here rather than cited inline. Matthew 4:1–11 and Luke 4:1–13 are cited because Origen names the Gospel account of the temptation, though he declines to use it. ἀποτροπιάζεσθαι (to avert evil by rite, to banish as ill-omened) is rendered ‘driven off to avert evil’.
'driven off as a thing to be averted' -> 'driven off to avert evil' (ἀποτροπιάζεσθαι; old wording was stiff)
'I pass over' -> 'For I pass over' (γάρ restored)
'I do not yet speak of the passages in Ezekiel spoken as though of' -> 'I say nothing yet of the passages in Ezekiel that speak as though of' (οὔπω λέγω; smoother English)

checked: Genesis 3:1, 3:5, 3:6, 3:23-24; Exodus 12:23 (LXX ὀλεθρεύων); Leviticus 16:8-10 (ἀποπομπαῖος); Judges 19:22 (LXX A Βελιαλ); Job 1:6, 2:1, 1:9-12, 2:4-6, 1:13-19, 2:7; Job 38:1 (LXX λαῖλαψ, νέφη); LXX Job 40:25-41:26 = English Job 41:1-34; Ezekiel 29:2-3, 32:2, 28:2-19; Isaiah 14:4-21; Nebuchadnezzar left uncited with reason in note

choices.choice: 6.43: Origen also names Nebuchadnezzar but gets no inline verse citation, because no single Ezekiel passage fits. The note gives the reason. This is a judgement call against the inline-citation rule.
